pointers.sentence: The registry keeps its applications and its models in two separate dictionaries, and the difference between them explains much of its behaviour (`django/apps/registry.py:Apps.__init__`).

It is filled by the model classes themselves, as each registers, and filing does not look at `app_configs`: a model is filed there whether or not its application is installed and whether or not the registry has been populated (`django/apps/registry.py:Apps.register_model`).

A model is filed there as its module is imported, and an import cannot safely be replayed, since it could run initialization code again (`django/apps/registry.py:Apps.__init__`, `django/apps/registry.py:Apps.set_installed_apps`).

A model is filed there as its module is imported, and an import cannot safely be replayed, since it could run initialization code again (`django/apps/registry.py:Apps.__init__`, `django/apps/registry.py:Apps.set_installed_apps`).

Only `ManagementUtility.execute` replaces the main registry's map, with an empty one, when `django.setup` fails under runserver's reloader ([Who calls `django.setup`](callers.md#the-development-server-may-start-broken)) (`django/core/management/__init__.py:ManagementUtility.execute`).
It is the same dictionary object and not a copy, so a model registered later still appears in its application's `models` (`django/apps/config.py:AppConfig.import_models`).

`Apps.get_model` goes through `app_configs` and the configuration's `models`, and finds only the models of installed applications; `Apps.get_registered_model` goes straight into `all_models`, and finds a model of an application that is not installed as well (`django/apps/registry.py:Apps.get_registered_model`).
The class statement of a model runs the metaclass `ModelBase.__new__`, and two of its steps call the registry directly (`django/db/models/base.py:ModelBase.__new__`).

It gives the registry the dotted name of the module the class is being defined in, and `Apps.get_containing_app_config` returns the installed application whose package contains it; where applications are nested and several match, the one with the longest name (`django/apps/registry.py:Apps.get_containing_app_config`).

`get_containing_app_config` first calls `Apps.check_apps_ready`, which, where there are settings to read, raises `AppRegistryNotReady` until every entry of `INSTALLED_APPS` has its configuration, and the class statement makes the call whatever its `Meta` says (`django/apps/registry.py:Apps.check_apps_ready`).
`Apps.register_model` files the class in `all_models` under its label and its lower-case name (`django/apps/registry.py:Apps.register_model`).

Django's answer is a general one: give the registry a function and the names of the models it needs, and the registry calls it when the last of them has been registered (`django/apps/registry.py:Apps.lazy_model_operation`).
When no pair is left, the function is called with the classes (`django/apps/registry.py:Apps.lazy_model_operation`, `django/apps/registry.py:Apps.do_pending_operations`).
When no pair is left, the function is called with the classes (`django/apps/registry.py:Apps.lazy_model_operation`, `django/apps/registry.py:Apps.do_pending_operations`).

The function a related field hands over, `resolve_related_class`, is defined inside `RelatedField.contribute_to_class`; it puts the class on the field in place of the string and sets up the other side of the relation, the attribute on Book through which its loans are reached (`django/db/models/fields/related.py:RelatedField.contribute_to_class`).
Related fields are the main user, through a small wrapper that resolves a name relative to the model that uses it (`django/db/models/fields/related.py:lazy_related_operation`).

The model signals are another: `ModelSignal`, the class of `pre_init`, `post_init`, `pre_save`, `post_save`, `pre_delete`, `post_delete` and `m2m_changed`, accepts a sender named by a string and connects the receiver when that model is registered (`django/db/models/signals.py:ModelSignal._lazy_method`).

A function waiting for a model that is never registered stays in `_pending_operations` for the life of the process, since nothing takes it out but that model's registration (`django/apps/registry.py:Apps.do_pending_operations`).

The mistake is reported by the system checks, one of which goes through what is still waiting in `_pending_operations` and, for a relation, names the field and says whether the application is missing or only the model ([The model checks](../models/checks.md#check_lazy_references)) (`django/core/checks/model_checks.py:_check_lazy_references`).

It finds the `AppConfig` by label, raising `LookupError` if no installed application has it, and asks the configuration, which looks the name up in lower case in its `models` and raises `LookupError` if it is not there (`django/apps/registry.py:Apps.get_model`, `django/apps/config.py:AppConfig.get_model`).

It finds the `AppConfig` by label, raising `LookupError` if no installed application has it, and asks the configuration, which looks the name up in lower case in its `models` and raises `LookupError` if it is not there (`django/apps/registry.py:Apps.get_model`, `django/apps/config.py:AppConfig.get_model`).

It leaves out two kinds unless asked for them: the models Django makes automatically for a many-to-many relation that names no intermediate model, and a model that has been swapped out for another by a setting, as the auth application's `User` is when `AUTH_USER_MODEL` names a different one (`django/apps/config.py:AppConfig.get_models`, `django/contrib/auth/models.py:User`).

Once the registry is ready, it also goes to every model of an installed application, unless swapped out, and expires the caches on its `_meta`, among them the lists of fields and relations that each model computes on demand and keeps (`django/apps/registry.py:Apps.clear_cache`, `django/db/models/options.py:Options._expire_cache`).

Once the registry is ready, it also goes to every model of an installed application, unless swapped out, and expires the caches on its `_meta`, among them the lists of fields and relations that each model computes on demand and keeps (`django/apps/registry.py:Apps.clear_cache`, `django/db/models/options.py:Options._expire_cache`).

Its reverse relations are a fact about every other model, and `Options` works them out for all models at once, the first time any model is asked, by going through `Apps.get_models` and collecting every field that points to a class (`django/db/models/options.py:Options._populate_directed_relation_graph`).

Asked before `models_ready` for a name that is not one of the model's own fields, `Options.get_field` raises `FieldDoesNotExist` rather than compute the reverse relations, which are unavailable until then (`django/db/models/options.py:Options.get_field`).
A model that `get_model` returns with `require_ready=False` may lack reverse accessors until the registry is fully populated (`docs/ref/applications.txt`).
The main one is made with `None` in place of a list, because it cannot be populated yet, and the constructor refuses `None` once the main registry exists (`django/apps/registry.py:Apps.__init__`).

That is `Options.default_apps` unless the model's `Meta` names another (`django/db/models/options.py:Options.default_apps`), and `default_apps` is the main registry, except while a test's `isolate_apps` has put a registry of its own there ([Settings for one test: `override_settings` and `TestContextDecorator`](../testing/test-decorators.md#the-other-changes)).

Those classes live in a `StateApps`, a subclass of `Apps` populated with stub configurations, one for each label, in which a model can also be unregistered and the whole registry cloned (`django/db/migrations/state.py:StateApps`).
